# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 24: Revolut Swapped Its Default AI, and the Hosting Bill Came to a Tenth


### A free-weights default for 2,000 engineers, a big open model priced on your desk, ChatGPT plans that hit the limit faster, and a meter on agent calls.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 27, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5AgsOyOexTokMZalVId7c1) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/WAuFFd6w6zU) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


This week:


**Free Weights Friday** prices a big open model on your desk.


**OpenAI** fixed a billing mistake, so the same work now uses more of your plan.


**Google** is putting a meter on its agent tools for Gmail, Calendar and Drive.


**Google’s TPU** is on SemiAnalysis’s public chip scoreboard, and


**CoreWeave** shows what timing does to the price of a data center. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency, led by


**Revolut** . Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## Free Weights Friday


Open models anyone can download, and what it costs to run them.


**The desk.** In October,


[Layer2C Labs](https://labs.layer2c.com/labs/studio-or-spark) ran the same build of DeepSeek’s


**V4 Flash** on two setups, each with


**256 GB** of memory. Setup one: a single


**Apple Mac Studio** with an M5 Ultra,


**$12,299** as tested. Setup two: two


**Nvidia DGX Sparks** wired together (one alone couldn’t fit the model),


**128 GB** each, listed at


**$13,900** for the pair before the cable. So the Mac was about


**$1,600 cheaper** for the same memory. With two agent sessions running at once, each turn was faster on the Spark pair (about 18 seconds against 35.5 on the Mac). The software differed too, so it isn’t a clean hardware race. The Mac saved money; the Sparks saved time on that one test.


**Less memory?** Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson was picking the best model for a


**48–64 GB** Nvidia RTX Spark, for one job: customizing Omarchy, his Linux (


[his post](https://x.com/dhh/status/2125845831051858053) ). Thinking Machines’


**Inkling 2 Mini** beat Alibaba’s


**Qwen 3.8** (the 27-billion-parameter one) on that Omarchy test. His


[eval](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy-local-ai/pull/117) itself ran on a 128 GB Spark. A win on one job, not a ranking for every job.


**Which model is it, anyway?** A startup called


[Modaic](https://x.com/modaicdev/status/2125851808501583918) timed TypeSafe’s assistant,


**Jev** , on


**9,984** prompts. From the timing, it thinks Jev is built on Alibaba’s


**Qwen 3.5** (the 35-billion-parameter version). TypeSafe hasn’t confirmed that.


**What $10 buys.** Assume the model reads three tokens for every one it writes, with no cache discount. On DeepSeek’s


**V4 Pro** , at


[DeepSeek’s own](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing) peak price, $10 buys about


**5 million** tokens. Off-peak it’s half price, so about


**10 million** . When we recorded, a Baidu promo on


[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813) worked out to about


**27 million** ; by Friday OpenRouter listed Baidu at the same price as DeepSeek’s peak, so check before you buy.


**Jevons, still winning.**


[OpenRouter says](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/is-jevons-paradox-holding/) that across its platform, token prices fell this year and total spending still rose, but spending has responded less to falling prices than it did earlier in the year. Jevons is still winning, just not by as much.


All this to drive a future with


**Squeezed Intelligence** , or SI: a model that wanted a server room, now on a desk.


**Our per-dollar verdict:** if you buy the box, check what fits and how fast it runs your job. If you pay by the token, compare hosts for the same model.


---


## The big stories


**OpenAI’s billing mistake, in your favor.** OpenAI’s Tibo Sottiaux


[posted](https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2125784147889393806) that a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 “incorrectly discounted” GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users. It’s fixed, so the same work uses more of your plan’s allowance: compared with last week, you’ll reach your limits


**40% faster on Astra** and


**25% faster on Sol** . Other models weren’t affected. OpenAI says the new models should still go further than GPT-6 Astra and 6.1 Sol, won’t charge for the difference on past usage, and is giving Go, Plus, Pro and Business users one usage reset to save for later. A second change is coming: from December, Plus, Pro and Business plans share one allowance across ChatGPT and Codex, measured in tokens, and Instant chat doesn’t count against it (


[OpenAI Help Center](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001625) ). ChatGPT Plus is still $20 a month.


**Our per-dollar verdict:** same $20, less work on those two models than last week, and from December, one pot for chat and code.


**A meter on your robots.** Google is setting quotas for its official Workspace tools for AI agents, the ones that reach Gmail, Calendar and Drive (


[Google’s usage tiers](https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/quota-usage-tiers) ). On the free Standard tier, each project gets up to


**5,000 requests a day** , for each product. For more, a company enrolls in the paid Scaled tier and asks for a quota increase. Google starts billing Scaled customers on


**April 1, 2027** , charging from the first successful request. (Ben says April 21 on the show; Google’s page says April 1.) Stay on Standard and you hit a cap instead of a bill.


**Did your agents surprise you?** On Monday,


[Bain](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-agents-are-spending-are-cfos-in-control/) published a survey of


**150** finance leaders, all at companies with more than


**$1 billion** in annual revenue.


**77%** reported unexpected or unbudgeted agent costs. Among teams piloting or deploying agents, only


**16%** said they could forecast next quarter’s agent costs within 10% of the real bill.


**Our per-dollar verdict:** forecast how often your agents will call the tools, not just how many tokens they’ll use.


**The chip scoreboard.** Google’s TPU is on


[InferenceX](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/) , SemiAnalysis’s public scoreboard for how well chips serve AI models (


[SemiAnalysis](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/tpu-strikes-the-king) ). Nvidia’s chips were already on it. A correction to yesterday: our Trainium result was for one model, on SemiAnalysis’s cost estimates, not rental quotes.


**And a red light on the dock.** The Financial Times reported that Nvidia halted server shipments to


**Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia** , where new export licenses just kicked in; Dell and Supermicro told buyers their orders wouldn’t ship. Reuters said it couldn’t immediately verify the report (


[Reuters, via The Manila Times](https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/11/27/business/foreign-business/nvidia-stops-server-shipments-to-4-southeast-asian-countrie) ), and it’s unclear how long the halt lasts.


**Our per-dollar verdict:** price each setup on the same job, and ask your provider where its next servers are coming from.


**Bonus: when you need it is part of the price.** On its November 10 earnings call (


[transcript](https://s205.q4cdn.com/133937190/files/content_files/CoreWeave-3Q26-Transcript-_1_.pdf) ), CoreWeave said it was selling some short-term capacity for


**more than $40 million a year per megawatt** . For new builds, on four- and five-year deals, pricing was moving to


**$20–25 million a year per megawatt** . It also said it is largely sold out through 2027. Need it soon? That’s the hotel price. Can wait for the building? That’s the lease.


**Our per-dollar verdict:** compare quotes for the capacity you need and the term you can commit to.


---


## The Department of Token Efficiency


**Cut one: Revolut.** Revolut’s AI operations lead, David Abitbol, presented results for


**2,000 engineers** (


[his talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ok6QdZHCcI8) ). They had run coding agents with a budget cap each, and some ran up thousands of dollars a month. Revolut made a free-weights model, Z.ai’s


**GLM 5.3** , the default for coding, with frontier models kept for exceptions. Abitbol estimates serving those engineers takes


**56 Nvidia B200s** . At his blended cost of about $0.30 per million tokens, with cache reads free, $10 covers roughly


**33 million tokens** (our arithmetic). Against Revolut’s old Anthropic and OpenAI bill, the hosting invoice came to


**a tenth** (


[The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/11/03/british-fintech-revolut-slashes-ai-coding-costs-10x-by-cutting-out-claude-and-going-self-hosted/5307345) ), and the self-hosted setup has no token limits.


**The fine print:** that’s one hosting invoice against the old provider spend, not the full cost per coding task.


**Cut two: Cloudflare.** Cloudflare built its own AI code reviewer, then watched the bill climb: between March and August, the inference cost of one review nearly doubled, and in its two worst weeks a review averaged about


**$2.43** . It reused more of its instructions from the cache and switched which models handle each part of the review. In its


[October write-up](https://blog.cloudflare.com/obsessive-inference-optimization) , the inference cost came down to


**77 cents** a review:


**68% less** than those worst weeks.


**The fine print:** Cloudflare tested its own reviewer, and its baseline is its two worst weeks.


**Cut three: Gaudiy.** Japanese tech company Gaudiy had one flagship GPU running around the clock for a single image feature, nearly


**90%** of its cloud bill (


[Gaudiy’s July write-up](https://techblog.gaudiy.com/entry/2026/07/31/203039) ). It switched to a smaller GPU at roughly a third of the price, added and removed capacity as the queue changed, and sized its servers to the job. Gaudiy says that feature’s production GPU cost fell by roughly


**three-quarters** .


**The fine print:** Gaudiy gave percentages for that one feature’s GPU cost, no dollar figures.
